title: The stored-program concept: EDVAC report, Manchester Baby, EDSAC
text:
CHAPTER 4. VACUUM TUBES AND THE FIRST ELECTRONIC COMPUTERS
SECTION 4.4. THE STORED-PROGRAM CONCEPT: EDVAC REPORT, MANCHESTER BABY, EDSAC

ENIAC proved that electronic computing was fast; it also proved that a machine programmed by rewiring wastes most of that speed waiting for people. The fix was to store the program as numbers in the machine's own fast memory, where it could be loaded in moments, read at electronic speed, and even modified by the program itself. This section explains the stored-program idea, the 1945 report that spread it, the memory technologies that made it possible, and the first two machines to run stored programs: the Manchester Baby (1948) and EDSAC (1949). Almost every computer since, including the CPUs and GPUs that train AI models, follows this design.

1. The idea

A stored-program computer keeps instructions and data in the same addressable read-write memory. Instructions are encoded as numbers. A control unit repeatedly:

    1. fetches the instruction at the address held in a program counter (PC);
    2. decodes it;
    3. executes it, reading or writing memory and registers as needed;
    4. updates the PC (to the next instruction, or to a jump target).

This is Turing's universal machine (Section 3.2) built as hardware: a fixed circuit that interprets a description held in memory.

Consequences:

  - Changing the program means loading new numbers into memory, which takes seconds instead of days.
  - Programs can compute addresses and alter instructions, which early machines used for loops and array access before index registers existed.
  - Programs can process other programs as data. That makes assemblers, compilers, loaders and operating systems possible, and, for AI, programs that generate or modify programs.

2. The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (1945)

While ENIAC was being built, its designers already knew its weaknesses. From 1944 Eckert, Mauchly and colleagues at the Moore School discussed a successor, the EDVAC (Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer), with a large memory based on mercury delay lines. John von Neumann (1903-1957), the Hungarian-American mathematician who was consulting for the Army, joined these discussions.

Von Neumann wrote a 101-page document, the "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC," which Herman Goldstine distributed on June 30, 1945. It described the logical design of a stored-program computer in abstract terms, using idealized neuron-like elements, explicitly citing the McCulloch-Pitts model (Section 7.2), rather than specific circuits. Its main points:

  - five components: a central arithmetic part, a central control, memory, input and output;
  - a single memory holding both instructions and numbers;
  - binary representation;
  - serial operation, one bit at a time, to economize on hardware.

The report was incomplete and carried only von Neumann's name. Because it was widely circulated, the design became known as the "von Neumann architecture." Eckert and Mauchly felt their contributions had been erased, and the public distribution also counted as publication that undermined patent claims on the stored-program idea. Historians today generally credit the concept to the Moore School team collectively, with von Neumann's report as its influential written expression. Eckert had already described storing instructions in a delay-line memory in a memo dated before von Neumann's involvement, and Zuse had mentioned a similar idea in a 1936 patent application. Turing's 1936 universal machine is the theoretical antecedent.

In the summer of 1946 the Moore School held a course on electronic computer design, the "Moore School Lectures," attended by people who went on to build computers in the US and Britain, including Maurice Wilkes of Cambridge, who attended the final weeks. This course spread the EDVAC design around the world. The EDVAC itself suffered delays after Eckert and Mauchly left and did not run reliably until around 1951, so it was not the first stored-program machine.

3. Turing's ACE

In late 1945, at the National Physical Laboratory (NPL) in London, Alan Turing completed a detailed design for a stored-program computer called the Automatic Computing Engine (ACE). The design was ambitious and original: it ran at a high clock rate for its time (1 MHz), used mercury delay line memory, and had many features later associated with RISC processors, such as a minimal set of simple instructions. Turing also wrote about subroutines and about the machine modifying its own instructions, and he speculated that it might be made to learn. The full ACE was never built, and Turing, frustrated with delays, left NPL. A smaller version, the Pilot ACE, became operational in 1950 and was for a time among the fastest computers in the world.

4. The memory problem

A stored-program machine needs memory that is large (hundreds to thousands of words), fast (microseconds), electronic and rewritable. Flip-flops made of tubes were fast but needed at least one or two tubes per bit, far too many for thousands of words. Two technologies made the first stored-program machines possible.

Mercury delay lines. Proposed for computing by Eckert, who had used them in radar. A tube of mercury, perhaps a meter or more long, has a piezoelectric quartz crystal at each end. Electrical pulses at one end become sound pulses traveling through the mercury at about 1.45 km/s; at the other end they are converted back to electrical pulses, amplified, reshaped and fed back into the input. A train of bits thus circulates continuously. With a delay of about 1 ms and a pulse rate of 500 kHz, one line stores about 500 bits.

    capacity (bits) = delay time * bit rate

It is serial-access memory: to read a word, you wait until it comes around. Average access time is half the circulation time, hundreds of microseconds, so programmers arranged instructions and data to come out of the line just when needed ("optimum coding"). Mercury had to be kept at a constant temperature, since sound speed varies with temperature.

The Williams-Kilburn tube. At the Telecommunications Research Establishment (TRE) in Britain, Freddie Williams and Tom Kilburn developed a way to store bits on the face of an ordinary cathode-ray tube (CRT). The electron beam writes a pattern of dots or dashes on the phosphor screen; each spot leaves a small electric charge that persists for a fraction of a second. A metal pickup plate on the outside of the screen detects the charge when the beam revisits a spot, so bits can be read, and must be periodically rewritten (refreshed). Any spot can be addressed by deflecting the beam, so it was random access, a great advantage over delay lines. By autumn 1947 they had stored 2,048 bits, a 64 by 32-bit array, and kept them for hours. Note the recurring concept: dynamic storage of charge that must be refreshed, as in Atanasoff's drum (Section 4.2) and in today's DRAM.

5. The Manchester Baby (1948)

To test the Williams tube in a real computing application, Williams, Kilburn and Geoff Tootill at the University of Manchester built a small experimental computer, the Small-Scale Experimental Machine (SSEM), nicknamed "Baby." On 21 June 1948 it became the first computer to run a program stored in its electronic read-write memory.

Its specifications were minimal:

  - memory: one Williams tube holding 32 words of 32 bits;
  - an accumulator and a control register (the program counter) on further Williams tubes;
  - seven instructions: jump (absolute and relative), load negative of a memory word into the accumulator, store the accumulator, subtract, skip next instruction if accumulator negative, and halt;
  - about 550 valves, 3.5 kW of power.

It had no addition, only subtraction; you add by subtracting a negative (a - (-b) = a + b). The first program, written by Kilburn, found the highest proper divisor of 2^18 = 262,144 by trying every integer downward from 2^18 - 1 and testing divisibility by repeated subtraction. It ran for 52 minutes and executed about 3.5 million instructions, around 1,100 instructions per second. The answer is 131,072 (that is, 2^17), but the point was to exercise the memory hard and long, proving the Williams tube reliable.

Why seven instructions are enough. With subtract, load negative, store, conditional skip and jump, you can build addition, loops and conditional branches, which is enough for Turing completeness (given more memory). This is a vivid demonstration of how little hardware general computation needs, the same lesson as small universal Turing machines.

The Baby led to the Manchester Mark 1 (1949), which introduced index registers (called "B-lines"), and then to the Ferranti Mark 1 (1951), among the first commercially available general-purpose computers. Turing joined Manchester in 1948 and wrote the programming manual for the Ferranti Mark 1. A working replica of the Baby is displayed at the Science and Industry Museum in Manchester.

6. EDSAC (1949)

Maurice Wilkes (1913-2010), director of the University of Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory, read von Neumann's report, attended the Moore School Lectures in 1946, and returned to Cambridge to build a practical machine to serve the university's scientists, the Electronic Delay Storage Automatic Calculator (EDSAC). Work started in 1947. On 6 May 1949 EDSAC ran its first programs, printing a table of the squares of the integers from 0 to 99, and then a list of prime numbers.

Specifications:

  - memory: mercury delay lines ("tanks"), 1,024 locations of 18 bits planned, with only 512 installed until 1952;
  - instruction format: a 5-bit operation code, a spare bit, a 10-bit address and a length bit choosing between 17-bit ("short") and 35-bit ("long") numbers;
  - an accumulator able to hold 71 bits, so two long numbers could be multiplied without loss;
  - input from punched paper tape, output on a teleprinter.

EDSAC was the first stored-program computer to provide a regular computing service to users, and the Cambridge group made it practical through software, which is its most important legacy:

  - Initial Orders, written by David Wheeler, a short program wired into read-only memory that read instructions from tape in a symbolic form, converted decimal addresses and loaded them: an early assembler and loader.
  - A subroutine library: tested routines for common operations such as square roots, printing and integration, called using the "Wheeler jump," a technique for subroutine call and return.
  - The book "The Preparation of Programs for an Electronic Digital Computer" (1951) by Wilkes, Wheeler and Stanley Gill, the first textbook on programming.

Wilkes also invented microprogramming in 1951: implementing the control unit as a small internal program of micro-instructions, which became standard in processors for decades. EDSAC was shut down on 11 July 1958, succeeded by EDSAC 2. EDSAC influenced LEO I, built by the J. Lyons catering company, which ran the first routine business computing jobs in 1951. A reconstruction of EDSAC has been built at The National Museum of Computing at Bletchley Park.

EDSAC has a place in AI and games history too: in 1952 A. S. (Sandy) Douglas wrote a noughts-and-crosses (tic-tac-toe) program for it, displaying the board on a CRT, as part of his PhD work on human-computer interaction.

7. The von Neumann bottleneck

The stored-program design has a built-in limitation: the processor and memory are separate, and every instruction and every operand must cross the connection between them. In his 1977 Turing Award lecture, John Backus, the creator of FORTRAN, called this the "von Neumann bottleneck."

It matters even more now than it did in 1948. Processor speeds grew much faster than memory speeds through the late twentieth century (the "memory wall"), so computers added caches (Section 6.4). For neural networks the problem is acute: each step of a large model must read billions of weight values from memory. In many AI workloads, moving data costs more time and energy than the arithmetic itself, which is why modern AI accelerators use high-bandwidth memory stacked next to the processor, large on-chip memories, and dataflow designs that reuse each value as many times as possible once fetched. Research into "in-memory computing," and the brain-inspired "neuromorphic" chips that mix memory and computation, is an attempt to escape the bottleneck that von Neumann's 1945 report defined.

8. Summary

  - A stored-program computer keeps instructions and data in one read-write memory and runs a fetch-decode-execute cycle; it is Turing's universal machine in hardware.
  - Von Neumann's "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" (distributed June 30, 1945) described the design and gave it his name, though it grew out of work with Eckert, Mauchly and the Moore School team.
  - Turing designed the ACE in 1945; the Pilot ACE ran in 1950.
  - Mercury delay lines (serial) and Williams-Kilburn CRT storage (random access, refreshed) supplied the first practical memories.
  - The Manchester Baby ran the first stored program on 21 June 1948 (32 words of 32 bits, seven instructions, 52-minute first run).
  - EDSAC (first programs 6 May 1949) gave the first regular stored-program computing service and pioneered assemblers, subroutine libraries and microprogramming.
  - The separation of memory and processing creates the von Neumann bottleneck, a central constraint of modern AI hardware.
